# What is Quarto?

[Quarto](https://quarto.org/) is a way to write reproducible reports that keep your explanations, R code, figures, tables, and results together. Quarto files use the `.qmd` extension and can produce HTML, PDF, Word, presentations, websites, and books.

Most of the file is ordinary text. R code only runs when it is placed inside an R code cell.

# Create your first file

Install [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/), R, and RStudio. In RStudio:

1. Select **File > New File > Quarto Document**.
2. Add a title and your name.
3. Choose HTML as the output format.
4. Select **Create**.

RStudio creates a sample document. You can delete the example content below the YAML header and start writing your own report.

::: {.callout-important}
Do not delete the opening and closing `---` lines. They define the document header.
:::

# Understand the header

The YAML header controls the title, author, date, output format, and document options.

```yaml
---
title: "My Quarto report"       # Document title
author: "Your name"             # Author name
date: today                     # Current date
toc: true                       # Add a table of contents
format:
  html:
    theme: flatly               # HTML appearance
    embed-resources: true       # Create one self-contained HTML file
execute:
  warning: false                # Hide warnings in the final document
  message: false                # Hide package messages
---
```

YAML indentation matters. Use spaces, keep nested options aligned, and do not use tabs.

# Create headings

Add `#` characters at the beginning of a line to create sections. More `#` characters create lower-level headings.

```markdown
# Main section

## Subsection

### Smaller subsection

#### Fourth-level heading

##### Fifth-level heading

###### Sixth-level heading
```

Use headings in order. A document normally starts with `#`, then uses `##` and `###` to organize related content.

# Add R code cells

Code cells are the places where you write executable R code. Everything outside a code cell is treated as text.

There are three common ways to insert an R cell:

1. Type ```` ```{r} ```` at the beginning and ```` ``` ```` at the end.
2. Press **Ctrl+Alt+I** on Windows or **Cmd+Option+I** on macOS.
3. Use the **Insert** button in the RStudio editor and select **R**.

```{r}
# Comments inside an R cell begin with #, just as they do in an R script.
x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
mean(x)
```

To run code without rendering the entire document:

- place the cursor on a line and press **Ctrl+Enter** on Windows or **Cmd+Enter** on macOS;
- click the green arrow in the upper-right corner of the code cell;
- use the **Run** menu in the RStudio editor.

Objects created in one cell are available to later cells during the same session and render.

# Control code and output

Cell options begin with `#|` and apply only to that cell.

```{r}
#| label: mpg-summary
#| echo: true

summary(mtcars$mpg)
```

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `#| echo: false` | Run the code but hide it |
| `#| output: false` | Hide printed output |
| `#| include: false` | Hide both code and output |
| `#| eval: false` | Display code without running it |
| `#| warning: false` | Hide warnings |
| `#| fig-width: 7` | Set figure width in inches |

Use inline R code when a value should update automatically:

```markdown
The mean fuel economy is `r round(mean(mtcars$mpg), 1)` miles per gallon.
```

The rendered result is: the mean fuel economy is `r round(mean(mtcars$mpg), 1)` miles per gallon.

# Format text

Quarto uses Markdown for ordinary writing.

```markdown
**Bold text**

*Italic text*

`code or an object name`

- an unordered list
- another item

1. the first step
2. the second step
```

The formatting appears as **bold text**, *italic text*, and `inline code` in the rendered document.

# Add links and images

Add a link with descriptive text followed by the URL:

```markdown
[RStudio and Posit cheat sheets](https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/)
```

Add an image with similar syntax, but place `!` at the beginning:

```markdown
![Alternative text](image.jpg)
```

The image can be a local file or a web URL. Local images should be stored inside the project and referenced with a relative path.

# Add tables and figures from R

Use `knitr::kable()` for a simple table:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cars
#| tbl-cap: "Average fuel economy by cylinder count"

car_summary <- aggregate(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean)
knitr::kable(
  car_summary,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Cylinders", "Mean MPG")
)
```

R graphics are inserted at the position of the code cell:

```{r}
#| label: fig-mpg-weight
#| fig-cap: "Heavier cars generally have lower fuel economy."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of car weight and fuel economy with a downward fitted line."

plot(
  mtcars$wt,
  mtcars$mpg,
  pch = 19,
  col = "#2878B5",
  xlab = "Weight (1,000 lb)",
  ylab = "Fuel economy (mpg)"
)
abline(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars), col = "#C82423", lwd = 2)
```

Labels beginning with `tbl-` or `fig-` can be referenced in the text. For example, @tbl-cars summarizes the cars and @fig-mpg-weight displays the relationship between weight and fuel economy.

# Add references and footnotes

Create a footnote with `[^1]` in the text and define it elsewhere in the document:

```markdown
Quarto supports footnotes.[^1]

[^1]: This is the footnote text.
```

For academic citations, add a BibTeX file to the header:

```yaml
bibliography: references.bib
```

Then cite an entry with `[@citation-key]`. Quarto creates the reference list automatically.

# Render the document

Click **Render** at the top of the RStudio editor. Quarto runs the code from top to bottom and creates the requested output.

You can also render from a terminal:

```{bash}
#| eval: false

quarto render index.qmd
```

Change the YAML to select another format:

```yaml
format: html
```

```yaml
format: docx
```

```yaml
format: pdf
```

PDF output requires a TeX installation. HTML is usually the easiest format for a first document.

Before sharing, restart R and render again. This confirms that the document loads every package, creates every object, and does not depend on items left in the interactive environment.
